title: Opera Singers and Singing Lemurs: Same Trick, Different Branch of the Tree of Life
summary:
In the rainforests of Madagascar, a primate belts out eerie, siren-like songs that echo for miles. It's called the indri, the world's only known singing lemur. And new research shows it hits those high notes using the same technique as a trained opera singer.

The study, published in PLOS Computational Biology, analyzed 83 video recordings of 19 wild indris. Using markerless motion-tracking technology, researchers followed the lemurs' upper and lower lips frame by frame, comparing mouth opening with changes in vocal pitch. The pattern was clear: the higher the note, the wider the mouth.

Human singers do the same thing. It's called "formant tuning" — widening the mouth to align with the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract, amplifying the sound. For the indri, this could be the difference between a song that carries through the thick rainforest and one that doesn't. That matters, because indri songs strengthen social bonds and warn neighboring groups to keep their distance.

"Every time the pitch of an indri's song rose, we could see its mouth opening wider, frame by frame," said Chiara De Gregorio, a primatologist at the University of Warwick and a study co-author. "It's the kind of fine-tuned coordination between voice and body that we usually associate with trained human singers, not with a lemur singing from the forest canopy."

Here's the twist: humans and indris last shared a common ancestor roughly 74 million years ago — long before the dinosaurs went extinct. So neither species learned this from the other. Instead, both arrived at the same solution independently, a phenomenon called convergent evolution.

"Applying markerless pose estimation to footage recorded in the wild allowed us to look not just at the sounds indris make, but at the physical movements behind them," added co-author Filippo Carugati of the University of Turin.

The finding suggests that the link between body movement and vocal power is far older and more widespread than anyone thought — a trick nature invented more than once.
why_it_matters: The study suggests that the connection between moving your body and controlling your voice is far older than humans — a piece of biological machinery that evolution invented more than once. It also shows how AI-style video analysis is changing field biology, letting scientists learn from wild animals without ever touching them.

background_read: Madagascar (a large island country off the southeast coast of Africa) broke away from the African mainland tens of millions of years ago, so most of its wildlife — including every species of lemur — lives nowhere else on Earth. That isolation makes Madagascar a natural laboratory for studying how unusual behaviours evolve.

The indri is the largest living lemur and one of the few primates famous for singing rather than calling. Its song travels through the forest canopy and is used to keep in touch with family groups and to tell neighbouring groups how far away they are.

The new study appeared in PLOS Computational Biology (a peer-reviewed journal that publishes research using computers, maths and data to understand living things), and the work involved scientists at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom and the University of Turin in Italy.

Convergent evolution — the same trick evolving twice in unrelated lineages — is one of biology's most striking patterns. Bats, birds and insects each evolved wings separately, and bats and dolphins each evolved echolocation on their own, with no shared ancestor teaching them how.

Researchers increasingly use markerless pose estimation, software that reads body movements straight from ordinary video, to study wild animals without trapping or tagging them. That shift lets scientists observe rare species in their real habitat, though samples often stay small.

perspectives.description: The finding is a clean example of convergent evolution: two lineages separated for about 74 million years reached the same vocal solution. It suggests that linking body posture to sound production is a very old and useful trick, not a special human talent.

The evidence rests on a small sample — 19 wild indris and 83 clips — and the link between mouth opening and volume is inferred rather than measured directly in the forest. Correlation between pitch and mouth width is suggestive, but it does not prove the indri sings louder or reaches further because of it.

Biology keeps finding the same designs in unrelated animals: wings, eyes, echolocation, and now vocal technique. Each case reminds scientists that shared ancestry is not the only way species end up looking and acting alike; similar problems can produce similar answers.

If pose-tracking software can reveal vocal technique in a rainforest lemur, it can be pointed at other singing or calling animals, from gibbons to whales. The next question is whether acoustic and physical coordination follows the same rules across species — and whether that knowledge can help protect animals whose communication depends on being heard.
